claim: There is a long-standing debate about whether categories are represented by individual category members (exemplars) or by the central tendency abstracted from individual members (prototypes).
source: There is a long-standing debate about whether categories are represented by individual category members (exemplars) or by the central tendency abstracted from individual members (prototypes).
evidence: This is a statement about the existence of a debate in the scientific literature, drawing from established scientific discourse.

claim: Neuroimaging studies have shown neural evidence for either exemplar representations or prototype representations, but not both.
source: Neuroimaging studies have shown neural evidence for either exemplar representations or prototype representations, but not both.
evidence: This statement summarizes prior neuroimaging literature on category representations.

claim: Under the right circumstances, individuals may form representations at multiple levels of specificity.
source: These findings indicate that, under the right circumstances, individuals may form representations at multiple levels of specificity, potentially facilitating a broad range of future decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the present study.

claim: Exemplar models propose that categories are represented by their individual category members.
source: Some propose that categories are represented by their individual category members and that generalizing the category label to new examples involves joint retrieval and consideration of individual examples encountered in the past (i.e., exemplar models, Figure 1A; Kruschke, 1992; Medin and Schaffer, 1978; Nosofsky, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on exemplar models.

claim: Prototype models propose that categories are represented by their central tendency.
source: Others propose that categories are represented by their central tendency – an abstract prototype containing all the most typical features of the category (i.e., prototype models, Figure 1B; Homa, 1973; Posner and Keele, 1968; Reed, 1972).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work on prototype models.

claim: Both prototype and exemplar accounts have been formalized as quantitative models and fit to behavioral data for decades.
source: Both the prototype and exemplar accounts have been formalized as quantitative models and fit to behavioral data for decades, with numerous studies supporting each model (exemplar meta-analysis: Nosofsky, 1988; prototype meta-analysis: Smith and Minda, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to meta-analyses of each model type.

claim: Studies using univariate contrasts showed overlap between neural systems supporting categorization and recognition.
source: Studies using univariate contrasts showed overlap between neural systems supporting categorization and recognition (Nosofsky et al., 2012), as well as medial temporal lobe involvement in categorization (Koenig et al., 2008; Lech et al., 2016; Nomura et al., 2007), both of which have been interpreted as indicating a role of exemplar retrieval in categorization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Medial temporal lobe is involved in categorization.
source: Studies using univariate contrasts showed overlap between neural systems supporting categorization and recognition (Nosofsky et al., 2012), as well as medial temporal lobe involvement in categorization (Koenig et al., 2008; Lech et al., 2016; Nomura et al., 2007), both of which have been interpreted as indicating a role of exemplar retrieval in categorization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Mack et al., 2013 found similar behavioral fits for prototype and exemplar models, but better fit of the exemplar model to brain data.
source: Mack et al., 2013 found similar behavioral fits for the two models, but better fit of the exemplar model to brain data.
evidence: This statement directly cites findings from Mack et al., 2013.

claim: Parts of the lateral occipital, lateral prefrontal and lateral parietal cortices tracked exemplar model predictors in Mack et al., 2013.
source: Parts of the lateral occipital, lateral prefrontal and lateral parietal cortices tracked exemplar model predictors.
evidence: This statement describes findings from Mack et al., 2013 as cited in the preceding context.

claim: No region tracked prototype predictors in Mack et al., 2013.
source: No region tracked prototype predictors.
evidence: This statement describes findings from Mack et al., 2013 as cited in the preceding context.

claim: Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018 found better fit of the prototype model in both brain and behavior.
source: In contrast, Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018 found better fit of the prototype model in both brain and behavior.
evidence: This statement directly cites findings from Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior hippocampus tracked prototype predictors in Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018.
source: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior hippocampus tracked prototype predictors, demonstrating that neural category representations can involve more than representing the individual category members, even in regions like the hippocampus typically thought to support memory for specific episodes.
evidence: This statement describes findings from Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018 as cited in the preceding context.

claim: Lateral prefrontal regions are thought to resolve interference between similar items in memory.
source: Lateral prefrontal regions are thought to resolve interference between similar items in memory (Badre and Wagner, 2005; Bowman and Dennis, 2016; Jonides et al., 1998; Kuhl et al., 2007), and lateral parietal cortex supports recollective experience (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008) and maintains high fidelity representations of individual items during memory retrieval (Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on lateral prefrontal function.

claim: Lateral parietal cortex supports recollective experience.
source: Lateral prefrontal regions are thought to resolve interference between similar items in memory (Badre and Wagner, 2005; Bowman and Dennis, 2016; Jonides et al., 1998; Kuhl et al., 2007), and lateral parietal cortex supports recollective experience (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008) and maintains high fidelity representations of individual items during memory retrieval (Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on lateral parietal function.

claim: Lateral parietal cortex maintains high fidelity representations of individual items during memory retrieval.
source: Lateral prefrontal regions are thought to resolve interference between similar items in memory (Badre and Wagner, 2005; Bowman and Dennis, 2016; Jonides et al., 1998; Kuhl et al., 2007), and lateral parietal cortex supports recollective experience (Vilberg and Rugg, 2008) and maintains high fidelity representations of individual items during memory retrieval (Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on lateral parietal function.

claim: The VMPFC and hippocampus support episodic inference through memory integration of related episodes.
source: In contrast, the VMPFC and hippocampus are known to support episodic inference through memory integration of related episodes (Schlichting et al., 2015; Shohamy and Wagner, 2008; Zeithamova et al., 2012) and encoding of new information in light of prior knowledge (van Kesteren et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on VMPFC and hippocampal function.

claim: The VMPFC and hippocampus support encoding of new information in light of prior knowledge.
source: In contrast, the VMPFC and hippocampus are known to support episodic inference through memory integration of related episodes (Schlichting et al., 2015; Shohamy and Wagner, 2008; Zeithamova et al., 2012) and encoding of new information in light of prior knowledge (van Kesteren et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on VMPFC and hippocampal function.

claim: Prior studies have compared different category structures and task instructions to identify multiple memory systems supporting categorization.
source: Prior studies have compared different category structures and task instructions to identify multiple memory systems supporting categorization (e.g., Aizenstein et al., 2000; Ashby et al., 1998; Ell et al., 2010; Zeithamova et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Mixed representations have been identified in episodic memory tasks, with individuals sometimes forming both integrated and separated representations for the same events.
source: Such mixed representations have been identified in episodic memory tasks, with individuals sometimes forming both integrated and separated representations for the same events (Schlichting et al., 2015) and a single episode sometimes represented at multiple levels of specificity, even within the hippocampus (Collin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on episodic memory.

claim: A single episode is sometimes represented at multiple levels of specificity, even within the hippocampus.
source: Such mixed representations have been identified in episodic memory tasks, with individuals sometimes forming both integrated and separated representations for the same events (Schlichting et al., 2015) and a single episode sometimes represented at multiple levels of specificity, even within the hippocampus (Collin et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Collin et al., 2015.

claim: Individuals sometimes use a mix of strategies in categorization, for example when most category members are classified according to a simple rule while others are memorized as exceptions to that rule.
source: We also know that individuals sometimes use a mix of strategies in categorization, for example when most category members are classified according to a simple rule while others are memorized as exceptions to that rule (Davis et al., 2012; Nosofsky et al., 1994).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on categorization strategies.

claim: Abstract representations that discard details of individual items are well suited to making generalization judgments but are poorly suited to judgments that require specificity.
source: These differing representations may emerge because they allow for flexibility in future decision-making, as abstract representations that discard details of individual items are well suited to making generalization judgments but are poorly suited to judgments that require specificity.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional properties of different types of representations.

claim: Prototype representations may emerge as a byproduct of retrieving category exemplars.
source: Alternatively, prototype representations may emerge as a byproduct of retrieving category exemplars, and they may themselves be encoded via recurrent connections, becoming an increasingly robust part of the concept representation (Hintzman, 1986; Koster et al., 2018; Zeithamova and Bowman, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to theoretical work on prototype formation.

claim: The present study used a training set with examples relatively close to the prototype, which has been shown to promote prototype abstraction.
source: This task used a training set with examples relatively close to the prototype, which has been shown to promote prototype abstraction (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018; Bowman and Zeithamova, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies showing this effect.

claim: Observational training tasks promote exemplar encoding.
source: To promote exemplar encoding, we used an observational training task rather than feedback-based training (Cincotta and Seger, 2007; Heindel et al., 2013; Poldrack et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies showing this effect.

claim: The prototype model predicts that subjects should be best at categorizing the prototypes themselves, with decreasing accuracy for items with fewer shared features with prototypes.
source: In behavior, the prototype model assumes that categories are represented by their prototypes and predicts that subjects should be best at categorizing the prototypes themselves, with decreasing accuracy for items with fewer shared features with prototypes.
evidence: This is a description of the predictions of the prototype model based on established theory.

claim: The prototype model does not make differential predictions for new and old (training) items at the same distance from the prototype.
source: The prototype model does not make differential predictions for new and old (training) items at the same distance from the prototype.
evidence: This is a description of the predictions of the prototype model based on established theory.

claim: The exemplar model predicts that subjects should be best at categorizing old items and new items closest to the old exemplars.
source: The exemplar model assumes that categories are represented by the previously encountered exemplars and predicts that subjects should be best at categorizing old items and new items closest to the old exemplars.
evidence: This is a description of the predictions of the exemplar model based on established theory.

claim: In Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018, participants' behavior was better explained by the prototype model than the exemplar model.
source: For example, in our prior study (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018), participants' behavior was better explained by the prototype model than the exemplar model, but we also observed an advantage for old items relative to new items at the same distance to prototypes, in line with exemplar but not prototype model predictions.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study by the authors.

claim: In Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018, an advantage for old items relative to new items at the same distance to prototypes was observed.
source: For example, in our prior study (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018), participants' behavior was better explained by the prototype model than the exemplar model, but we also observed an advantage for old items relative to new items at the same distance to prototypes, in line with exemplar but not prototype model predictions.
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study by the authors.

claim: Memory consolidation research suggests that memories become abstract over time, often at the expense of memory for specific details.
source: Notably, memory consolidation research suggests that memories become abstract over time, often at the expense of memory for specific details (McClelland et al., 1995; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Payne et al., 2009; Posner and Keele, 1970), suggesting that early concept representations may be exemplar-based.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on memory consolidation.

claim: Research on schema-based memory shows that abstract knowledge facilitates learning of individual items by providing an organizational structure into which new information can be incorporated.
source: In contrast, research on schema-based memory shows that abstract knowledge facilitates learning of individual items by providing an organizational structure into which new information can be incorporated (Bransford and Johnson, 1972; Tse et al., 2007; van Kesteren et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research on schema-based memory.

claim: The brain may form abstract and specific representations in parallel without trade-off between concept knowledge and memory for individual items.
source: Finally, abstract and specific representations need not trade-off in either direction. Instead, the brain may form these representations in parallel (Collin et al., 2015; Schlichting et al., 2015) without trade-off between concept knowledge and memory for individual items (Schapiro et al., 2017), generating the prediction that both prototype and exemplar representations may grow in strength over the course of learning.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Participants underwent fMRI scanning while learning two novel categories or 'species,' which were represented by cartoon animals varying on eight binary dimensions.
source: In the present study, participants underwent fMRI scanning while learning two novel categories or 'species,' which were represented by cartoon animals varying on eight binary dimensions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: The learning phase consisted of two types of runs: observational study runs and interim generalization test runs.
source: The learning phase consisted of two types of runs: observational study runs and interim generalization test runs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: During study runs, participants passively viewed individual category members with their accompanying species label.
source: During study runs, participants passively viewed individual category members with their accompanying species label ('Febble' or 'Badoon').
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: All of the items presented during study runs differed by two features from their respective prototypes.
source: All of the items presented during study runs differed by two features from their respective prototypes (for example, exemplars depicted in Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: Across the entire learning phase, there were four study-test cycles.
source: Across the entire learning phase, there were four study-test cycles, with different new test items at every cycle.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the present study.

claim: A reliable typicality gradient was observed where accuracy decreased with the distance from the prototypes during interim tests.
source: To summarize, we observed a reliable typicality gradient where accuracy decreased with the distance from the prototypes and both old and new items at the distance two numerically fell between distance 1 and distance three items (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results from the present study.

claim: The categorization gradient driven by higher accuracy for items closer to category prototypes observed during learning was also strong during the final test.
source: Thus, the categorization gradient driven by higher accuracy for items closer to category prototypes observed during learning was also strong during the final test.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from statistical results in the present study.

claim: The numeric advantage for old relative to new items was not statistically significant in the final test.
source: In contrast, a paired t-test for accuracy on old relative to new items at distance two showed that the numeric advantage for old relative to new items was not statistically significant in the final test [t(28)=0.93, p=0.36, CI95[−0.03,.08], d = 0.22].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the present study's data analysis.

claim: In the first half of learning, the majority of subjects (66%) had similar prototype and exemplar model fits.
source: In the first half of learning, the majority of subjects (66%) had similar prototype and exemplar model fits.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral model fitting analysis in the present study.

claim: In the second half of learning, the majority of subjects (56%) were best fit by the prototype model.
source: In the second half of learning and the final test, the majority of subjects (56% and 66%, respectively) were best fit by the prototype model.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral model fitting analysis in the present study.

claim: In the final test, the majority of subjects (66%) were best fit by the prototype model.
source: In the second half of learning and the final test, the majority of subjects (56% and 66%, respectively) were best fit by the prototype model.
evidence: This is a result from the behavioral model fitting analysis in the present study.

claim: The prototype model provided a significant advantage over the exemplar model in the final test.
source: When we compared prototype and exemplar model fits in the final test, we again found a significant advantage for the prototype model over the exemplar model [t(28)=3.53, p=0.001, CI95[0.89, 3.39], d = 0.23].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral model fitting analysis in the present study.

claim: The prototype model provided an overall better fit to behavioral responses throughout the learning phase and final test.
source: Thus, the prototype model provided an overall better fit to behavioral responses throughout the learning phase and final test, and the effect size of the prototype advantage was largest in the final test.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral model fitting results from the present study.

claim: The effect size of the prototype advantage was largest in the final test.
source: Thus, the prototype model provided an overall better fit to behavioral responses throughout the learning phase and final test, and the effect size of the prototype advantage was largest in the final test.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral model fitting results from the present study.

claim: There was a significant ROI x Model interaction effect during the learning phase.
source: As predicted, there was a significant ROI x Model interaction effect, indicating that there were differences across regions in the type of category information that they tracked.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study, as shown in Table 1.

claim: The VMPFC significantly tracked prototype information during the learning phase.
source: Consistent with prior work (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018), the VMPFC and anterior hippocampus (our predicted prototype regions) significantly tracked prototype information [VMPFC: t(28) = 2.86, p=0.004, CI95[µ >0.06], d = 0.75]; [anterior hippocampus: t(28) = 1.88, p=0.04, CI95[µ >0.009], d = 0.49].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: The anterior hippocampus significantly tracked prototype information during the learning phase.
source: Consistent with prior work (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018), the VMPFC and anterior hippocampus (our predicted prototype regions) significantly tracked prototype information [VMPFC: t(28) = 2.86, p=0.004, CI95[µ >0.06], d = 0.75]; [anterior hippocampus: t(28) = 1.88, p=0.04, CI95[µ >0.009], d = 0.49].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: Lateral parietal cortex significantly tracked exemplar model predictions during the learning phase.
source: For the predicted exemplar regions, we found that both lateral parietal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus significantly tracked exemplar model predictions [lateral parietal: t(28) = 2.06, p=0.02, CI95[µ >0.02], d = 0.54]; [inferior frontal: t(28) = 2.40, p=0.01, CI95[µ >0.03], d = 0.63], with numerically positive exemplar correlates in lateral occipital cortex that were not statistically significant [t(28)=0.78, p=0.22, CI95[µ >−0.05], d = 0.20].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: Inferior frontal gyrus significantly tracked exemplar model predictions during the learning phase.
source: For the predicted exemplar regions, we found that both lateral parietal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus significantly tracked exemplar model predictions [lateral parietal: t(28) = 2.06, p=0.02, CI95[µ >0.02], d = 0.54]; [inferior frontal: t(28) = 2.40, p=0.01, CI95[µ >0.03], d = 0.63], with numerically positive exemplar correlates in lateral occipital cortex that were not statistically significant [t(28)=0.78, p=0.22, CI95[µ >−0.05], d = 0.20].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: There was a significant exemplar advantage in lateral parietal cortex during the learning phase.
source: When comparing neural exemplar fits to neural prototype fits, there was a significant exemplar advantage in both lateral parietal cortex [t(28)=3.00, p=0.003, d = 0.71, CI95[µ >0.09]], and in inferior frontal gyrus [t(28)=2.63, p=0.01, d = 0.67, CI95[µ >0.06]], that did not reach significance in the lateral occipital cortex [t(28)=1.44, p=0.08, d = 0.36, CI95[µ >−0.06]].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: There was a significant exemplar advantage in inferior frontal gyrus during the learning phase.
source: When comparing neural exemplar fits to neural prototype fits, there was a significant exemplar advantage in both lateral parietal cortex [t(28)=3.00, p=0.003, d = 0.71, CI95[µ >0.09]], and in inferior frontal gyrus [t(28)=2.63, p=0.01, d = 0.67, CI95[µ >0.06]], that did not reach significance in the lateral occipital cortex [t(28)=1.44, p=0.08, d = 0.36, CI95[µ >−0.06]].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: Both the VMPFC and anterior hippocampus continued to significantly track prototype predictors during the final test.
source: As in the learning phase, both the VMPFC and anterior hippocampus continued to significantly track prototype predictors during the final test with effect sizes similar to those observed during learning [VMPFC: t(28) = 2.83, p=0.004, CI95[µ >0.06], d = 0.74]; [anterior hippocampus: t(28) = 1.98, p=0.03, CI95[µ >0.01], d = 0.52].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: Prototype correlates were significantly stronger than exemplar correlates in the anterior hippocampus during the final test.
source: Here, prototype correlates were significantly stronger than exemplar correlates in the anterior hippocampus [t(28)=2.28, p=0.02, d = 0.63], CI95[µ >0.02] and marginally stronger in the VMPFC [t(28)=1.67, p=0.053, d = 0.46, CI95[µ > - 0.03]].
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: Exemplar correlates did not reach significance in any of the predicted exemplar regions during the final test.
source: However, exemplar correlates did not reach significance in any of the predicted exemplar regions (all t < 1.18, p>0.12, d < 0.31).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the fMRI analysis in the present study.

claim: Signatures of both exemplar and prototype representations were found across distinct brain regions when participants categorized items during the learning phase.
source: We found signatures of both types of representations across distinct brain regions when participants categorized items during the learning phase.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI results from the present study.

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior hippocampus tracked abstract prototype information during the learning phase.
source: Consistent with predictions based on prior studies, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior hippocampus tracked abstract prototype information, and the inferior frontal gyrus and lateral parietal cortex tracked specific exemplar information.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI results from the present study.

claim: The inferior frontal gyrus and lateral parietal cortex tracked specific exemplar information during the learning phase.
source: Consistent with predictions based on prior studies, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and anterior hippocampus tracked abstract prototype information, and the inferior frontal gyrus and lateral parietal cortex tracked specific exemplar information.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI results from the present study.

claim: There was no evidence of representational shifts either from specific to abstract or vice versa across learning.
source: We did not find evidence of representational shifts either from specific to abstract or vice versa.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from the present study.

claim: Both types of representations emerged together during learning, although prototype correlates came to dominate by the final test.
source: Instead, results suggested that both types of representations emerged together during learning, although prototype correlates came to dominate by the final test.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from the present study.

claim: Specific and abstract representations may exist in parallel for the same categories.
source: Together, we show that specific and abstract representations may instead exist in parallel for the same categories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the present study.

claim: Using neuroimaging allowed detection of both types of representations apparent across different parts of the brain.
source: However, using neuroimaging allowed us to detect both types of representations apparent across different parts of the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the present study.

claim: The present study helps to resolve between prior neuroimaging studies fitting prototype and exemplar models to brain data.
source: In addition to contributing novel findings to a longstanding debate in the behavioral literature, the present study also helps to resolve between prior neuroimaging studies fitting prototype and exemplar models to brain data.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the present study.

claim: Neural prototype and exemplar correlates can exist not only across different task contexts but also within the same task.
source: The present data newly show that neural prototype and exemplar correlates can exist not only across different task contexts but also within the same task, providing evidence that these neural differences reflect distinct category representations rather than different task details.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the present study.

claim: Integrating across experiences may serve to derive abstract information such as category prototypes.
source: That is, integrating across experiences may not only link related elements as in episodic inference tasks, but may also serve to derive abstract information such as category prototypes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the present findings in the context of prior work.

claim: The present findings are consistent with a proposed gradient along the hippocampal long axis, with representations becoming increasingly coarse in spatial and temporal scale moving from posterior to anterior portions of the hippocampus.
source: Our findings are consistent with a proposed gradient along the hippocampal long axis, with representations becoming increasingly coarse in spatial and temporal scale moving from posterior to anterior portions of the hippocampus (Brunec et al., 2018; Poppenk et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement relates the present findings to prior theoretical work, supported by citations.

claim: IFG is thought to play a critical role in resolving interference between similar items.
source: In particular, IFG is thought to play a critical role in resolving interference between similar items (Badre and Wagner, 2005; Bowman and Dennis, 2016; Jonides et al., 1998; Kuhl et al., 2007) while lateral parietal cortices often show high fidelity representations of individual items and features necessary for task performance (Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on IFG function.

claim: Lateral parietal cortices often show high fidelity representations of individual items and features necessary for task performance.
source: In particular, IFG is thought to play a critical role in resolving interference between similar items (Badre and Wagner, 2005; Bowman and Dennis, 2016; Jonides et al., 1998; Kuhl et al., 2007) while lateral parietal cortices often show high fidelity representations of individual items and features necessary for task performance (Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies on lateral parietal function.

claim: Regions supporting memory specificity across many memory tasks may also contribute to exemplar-based concept learning.
source: The present findings support and further this prior work by showing that regions supporting memory specificity across many memory tasks may also contribute to exemplar-based concept learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the present findings in the context of prior work.

claim: Representations in visual regions shift with category learning.
source: This prediction was based both on its previously demonstrated exemplar correlates in the Mack et al. study as well as evidence that representations in visual regions shift with category learning (Folstein et al., 2013; Freedman et al., 2001; Myers and Swan, 2012; Palmeri and Gauthier, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: All stimulus features in the present study were equally relevant for determining category membership.
source: However, in contrast to this prior work, all stimulus features in our study were equally relevant for determining category membership.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the present study.

claim: The aspect of the task where all features were equally relevant may have limited the role of selective attention in the present study.
source: This aspect of our task may have limited the role of selective attention in the present study and thus the degree to which perceptual regions tracked category information.
evidence: This is speculation about why certain results were obtained.

claim: In Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018, the prototype model fit reliably better than the exemplar model in 73% of the sample.
source: In designing the present study, we aimed to increase exemplar strategy use as compared to our prior study in which the prototype model fit reliably better than the exemplar model in 73% of the sample (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018).
evidence: This statement describes findings from a prior study by the authors.

claim: The present study included a relatively coherent category structure that was likely to promote prototype formation.
source: We included a relatively coherent category structure that was likely to promote prototype formation (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018; Bowman and Zeithamova, 2020), but tried to balance it with an observational rather than feedback-based training task in hopes of emphasizing individual items and promoting exemplar representations.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the present study, supported by citations.

claim: The results suggest some shift in model fits, albeit modest.
source: The results suggest some shift in model fits, albeit modest.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral model fitting results from the present study.

claim: The behavioral shift in model fits may have been sufficient to make exemplar representations detectable despite prototype dominance in behavior.
source: Thus, while the behavioral shift in model fits was modest, it may have been sufficient to make exemplar representations detectable despite prototype dominance in behavior.
evidence: This is speculation about the relationship between behavioral and neural results.

claim: Representations may form at multiple levels of specificity to promote flexibility in future decision-making.
source: It may be that representations form at multiple levels of specificity to promote flexibility in future decision-making because it is not always clear what aspects of current experience will become relevant (Zeithamova and Bowman, 2020).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Category representations can spontaneously form alongside memory for individuals, even when task instructions emphasize distinguishing between similar individuals.
source: Consistent with this idea, research shows that category representations can spontaneously form alongside memory for individuals, even when task instructions emphasize distinguishing between similar individuals (Ashby et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Accessing prototype representations may be efficient for making generalization judgments, but they cannot on their own support judgments that require discrimination between separate experiences or between members of the same category.
source: In the present context, accessing prototype representations may be efficient for making generalization judgments, but they cannot on their own support judgments that require discrimination between separate experiences or between members of the same category.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional properties of prototype representations.

claim: Exemplar representations may form to support judgments requiring specificity.
source: Thus, exemplar representations may also form to support judgments requiring specificity.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of exemplar representations.

claim: Neuroimaging studies of spatial processing, episodic inference, and memory for narratives have shown evidence for separate representations of individual experiences alongside representations that integrate across experiences.
source: Precedence for co-existing representations also comes from neuroimaging studies of spatial processing (Brunec et al., 2018), episodic inference (Schlichting et al., 2015), and memory for narratives (Collin et al., 2015). These studies have all shown evidence for separate representations of individual experiences alongside representations that integrate across experiences.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior neuroimaging studies.

claim: Co-existing prototype and exemplar representations were clear during the learning phase but not present during the final test phase.
source: While co-existing prototype and exemplar representations were clear during the learning phase of our task, they were not present during the final test phase.
evidence: This is a summary of the fMRI results from the present study.

claim: The lack of exemplar correlates in the brain during the final test was matched by a weaker exemplar effect in behavior.
source: The lack of exemplar correlates in the brain was matched by a weaker exemplar effect in behavior.
evidence: This is a summary of the results from the present study.

claim: Exemplar representations may have been weakened in the absence of further observational study runs that had boosted exemplars in earlier phases.
source: One possibility is that exemplar representations were weakened in the absence of further observational study runs that had boosted exemplars in earlier phases.
evidence: This is speculation about why exemplar correlates disappeared in the final test.

claim: Framing the test as a 'final test' may have switched participants from trying to gather multiple kinds of information to simply deploying the strongest representation that they had.
source: Similarly, framing it as a 'final test' may have switched participants from trying to gather multiple kinds of information that might improve later performance (i.e., both exemplar and prototype) to simply deploying the strongest representation that they had, which seems to have been prototype-based.
evidence: This is speculation about why exemplar correlates disappeared in the final test.

claim: Exemplar representations may increase up to some threshold while individuals are encoding complex stimuli, then decrease as a result of repetition suppression once individual items are sufficiently well represented.
source: Alternatively, there may be real, non-linear dynamics in how prototype and exemplar representations develop. For example, exemplar representations may increase up to some threshold while individuals are encoding these complex stimuli, then decrease as a result of repetition suppression (Desimone, 1996; Gonsalves et al., 2005; Henson et al., 2002) once individual items are sufficiently well represented.
evidence: This is speculation about representational dynamics, supported by citations to work on repetition suppression.

claim: Individuals may use both rules and memory for individual exemplars throughout learning without strong shifts from one to the other.
source: Prior work has shown that individuals may use both rules and memory for individual exemplars throughout learning without strong shifts from one to the other (Thibaut et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Early learning may be focused on detecting simple rules and testing multiple hypotheses.
source: Others have suggested that there may be representational shifts during category learning, but rather than shifting between exemplar and prototype representations, early learning may be focused on detecting simple rules and testing multiple hypotheses (Johansen and Palmeri, 2002; Nosofsky et al., 1994; Paniukov and Davis, 2018), whereas similarity-based representations such as prototype and exemplar representations may develop later in learning (Johansen and Palmeri, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Similarity-based representations such as prototype and exemplar representations may develop later in learning.
source: Others have suggested that there may be representational shifts during category learning, but rather than shifting between exemplar and prototype representations, early learning may be focused on detecting simple rules and testing multiple hypotheses (Johansen and Palmeri, 2002; Nosofsky et al., 1994; Paniukov and Davis, 2018), whereas similarity-based representations such as prototype and exemplar representations may develop later in learning (Johansen and Palmeri, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The present findings are consistent with a framework where strong prototype and exemplar representations emerge across distinct regions primarily in the second half of learning.
source: Our findings are consistent with this framework, with strong prototype and exemplar representations emerging across distinct regions primarily in the second half of learning.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the present findings in the context of prior theoretical work.

claim: The present results are consistent with recent neuroimaging studies showing multiple memory representations forming in parallel without need for competition.
source: Our results are also consistent with recent neuroimaging studies showing multiple memory representations forming in parallel without need for competition (Collin et al., 2015; Schlichting et al., 2015), potentially allowing individuals to flexibly use prior experience based on current decision-making demands.
evidence: This statement relates the present findings to prior neuroimaging studies, supported by citations.

claim: Multiple types of category representations may co-exist across distinct brain regions within the same categorization task.
source: In the present study, we found initial evidence that multiple types of category representations may co-exist across distinct brain regions within the same categorization task.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the present study.

claim: The regions identified as prototype-tracking and exemplar-tracking in the present study align with prior studies that have found only one or the other.
source: The regions identified as prototype-tracking (anterior hippocampus and VMPFC) and exemplar-tracking (IFG and lateral parietal cortex) in the present study align with prior studies that have found only one or the other.
evidence: This is a summary of how the present findings relate to prior work.

claim: The present findings shed light on the multiple memory systems that contribute to concept representation.
source: These findings shed light on the multiple memory systems that contribute to concept representation and provide novel evidence of how the brain may flexibly represent information at different levels of specificity and that these representations may not always compete during learning.
evidence: This is a claim about the contribution of the present study.

claim: The present findings provide novel evidence of how the brain may flexibly represent information at different levels of specificity.
source: These findings shed light on the multiple memory systems that contribute to concept representation and provide novel evidence of how the brain may flexibly represent information at different levels of specificity and that these representations may not always compete during learning.

source: These findings shed light on the multiple memory systems that contribute to concept representation and provide novel evidence of how the brain may flexibly represent information at different levels of specificity and that these representations may not always compete during learning.

source: This sample size was determined based on effect sizes for neural prototype-tracking and exemplar-tracking regions estimated from prior studies (Bowman and Zeithamova, 2018; Mack et al., 2013), allowing for detection of the minimum effect size (prototype correlates in anterior hippocampus, d = 0.43 with n = 29) using a one-tailed, one-sample t-test with at least 80% power.

claim: Stimuli consisted of cartoon animals that differed on eight binary features.
source: Stimuli consisted of cartoon animals that differed on eight binary features: neck (short vs. long), tail (straight vs. curled), foot shape (claws vs. round), snout (rounded vs. pig), head (ears vs. antennae), color (purple vs. red), body shape (angled vs. round), and design on the body (polka dots vs. stripes) (Bozoki et al., 2006; Zeithamova et al., 2008; available for download osf.io/8bph2).

source: The training set included four stimuli per category, each differing from their category prototype by two features (see Table 2 for training set structure).

source: The training set structure was selected to generate many pairs of training items that were four features apart both within the same category and across the two categories.
